INTRODUCTION

介绍

In July 2021, I was diagnosed with malignant eye cancer. Thankfully , it was early stage, and it appears that the medical therapy worked well.

2021年7月，我被诊断出患有恶性眼癌。幸运的是，病情发展到早期，而且药物治疗似乎效果很好。

The cliché is that this brief encounter with death would have led me to live every day as if it were the last. It didn’t. It never does.

人们常说，这次与死神短暂的相遇会让我把每一天都当作最后一天来过。但事实并非如此。也从来都不是。

People who are reminded of their mortality are often shaken up from their routine, yes, but never really live their day as if it were the last one. 1 Because doing so would be suboptimal if there’s more than one day left.

那些被提醒自己终将一死的人，往往会打破常规，没错，但他们永远不会真正像过最后一天那样去生活。因为如果还剩下不止一天，这样做就不是最佳选择。

In fact, all our decisions are underpinned by an implicit assumption of a time horizon for which to optimize. Whether to do unpaid work is influenced by how long we think a work relationship will last. Whether to marry our romantic partner is influenced by how long we believe our love will last. 2

事实上，我们所有的决定都隐含着一个需要优化的时间范围假设。是否从事无偿工作取决于我们认为工作关系能持续多久。是否与伴侣结婚取决于我们相信爱情能持续多久。

Time horizons are the basis of our decisions – and of our regrets. Live as if you would die tomorrow, and you will regret not having pursued long-term engagements (such as fulfilling professional ambitions, building a family, and so on). But live as if you couldn’t die, and you will regret not having done what you cannot do anymore.

时间观念是我们做决定的基础，也是我们后悔的基础。如果你活得好像明天就要死去，你就会后悔没有追求长远目标（例如实现职业抱负、组建家庭等等）。但如果你活得好像不会死，你就会后悔没有去做那些你再也做不了的事情。

Getting the time horizon right is fundamental for a life with few regrets. Sadly , there’s too much variance and too many unknowns for us to get it reliably right. However , we can improve our outcomes by understanding the effect of time and variance on our choices – and making choices that do not need our guess to be exact to work out.

把握好时间跨度对于减少人生遗憾至关重要。遗憾的是，由于变数太多、未知因素太多，我们无法始终准确把握。然而，我们可以通过了解时间和变数对我们选择的影响，并做出无需精确预测就能奏效的选择，从而改善我们的结果。

Ergodicity is the field of study that concerns itself with precisely that. And reading this book will help you make better decisions – decisions that don’t ignore time but leverage it, decisions that minimize regret and yet maximize long-term potential.

遍历性正是研究这一问题的领域。阅读本书将帮助你做出更明智的决策——这些决策不会忽视时间，而是充分利用时间；这些决策能够最大限度地减少遗憾，同时最大限度地发挥长期潜力。

A note about this book

关于这本书的说明

I wrote this book to explain the relevance of ergodicity to readers interested in its practical applications but not in its mathematical foundations.

我写这本书是为了向对遍历性的实际应用感兴趣但对其数学基础不感兴趣的读者解释遍历性的意义。

In the inevitable tradeoff between formal precision and accessibility, I favored the latter. Therefore , this book contains sentences that are correct in their practical meaning but technically imprecise. I use footnotes to reference justifications and more precise formulations.

在形式上的精确性和易读性之间不可避免的权衡中，我选择了后者。因此，本书中有些句子在实际意义上是正确的，但在技术上不够精确。我使用脚注来解释其合理性并提供更精确的表述。

Sometimes , I edited quotes for punctuation. Emphasis is always mine.

有时我会修改引语中的标点符号。强调部分始终是我加的。

Enjoy this book!

好好享受这本书吧！

PART I
第一部分
# ↩

LOSSES ABSORB FUTURE GAINS

损失会吸收未来的收益

Ever since a young age, we are taught that a cost-benefit analysis determines whether it is a good idea to do something. If the gains are larger than the losses, then go ahead.

我们从小就被教导，成本效益分析可以决定做某件事是否明智。如果收益大于损失，那就去做。

The real world begs to differ. There are cases in which it is a terrible idea to do something whose gains are larger than its losses. 1 The next chapter tells the story of how my cousin learned this lesson during his short-lived career as a professional skier.

但现实世界却并非如此。有些情况下，做某件事的收益大于损失，反而会适得其反。下一章将讲述我的表弟在他短暂的职业滑雪生涯中是如何吸取这个教训的。

1 This applies to “Russian Roulette situations” – a concept explained in the chapter after the next.

1 这适用于“俄罗斯轮盘赌情况”——这一概念将在下一章中解释。

# ↩
1
# ↩

IT IS NOT THE FASTEST SKIER THAT WINS RACES

赢得比赛的并非速度最快的滑雪者。

M y cousin was born in a mountain village in the French Alps . Like many there, he learned to ski before reading. I am a good skier, but I remember the humiliation when I was 14 and he was 6, seeing him surpass me, swift as a bullet. At a young age, he made it into the World Championships for his age bracket. Boy , he was fast!

我的表弟出生在法国阿尔卑斯山的一个山村。和那里许多人一样，他先学会了滑雪，才学会读书。我滑雪滑得不错，但我还记得14岁那年，他6岁，我被他轻松超越时的那种羞辱感，他滑得像子弹一样快。小小年纪，他就参加了同年龄组的世界锦标赛。哇，他真是太快了！

His career ended abruptly a decade later, one leg injury at a time, until he had to retire before his twenties. From him, I learned that the skiers that you see on TV , the fastest racers in the world, didn’t get there because they were the fastest.

十年后，他的职业生涯戛然而止，腿伤不断，最终在他二十岁出头就不得不退役。从他身上，我了解到，你在电视上看到的那些滑雪运动员，那些世界上速度最快的选手，并不是因为他们速度最快才取得如此成就的。

They got there because they were the fastest of those who didn’t get injured into retirement.

他们之所以能取得这样的成就，是因为他们是那些没有因伤退役的人中速度最快的。

In skiing, and life in general, it is not the best ones who succeed. It is the best ones of those who survive.

在滑雪运动中，乃至在生活中，最终成功的并非最优秀的人，而是那些生存下来的人中最优秀的人。

# ↩
2
# ↩

PERFORMANCE VS. SURVIVAL

表现 vs. 生存

I n theory, performance determines success. The fastest skier wins the race, and the most performing employee becomes the most successful one.

理论上，绩效决定成功。滑雪速度最快的人赢得比赛，绩效最好的员工也成为最成功的员工。

In practice, performance is subordinate to survival . It is the fastest racer of those who survive that wins races, it is the highest performing employee who doesn’t burn out that becomes the most successful, and so on.

实际上，绩效服从于生存。只有那些能够生存下来的速度最快的赛车手才能赢得比赛，只有那些绩效最高且不会精疲力竭的员工才能获得最大的成功，以此类推。

I’m not just making the banal point that survival matters. I’m saying it matters more than performance . 1

我说的不仅仅是“生存很重要”这种老生常谈的观点。我是说，生存比表现更重要。

On the next page, let’s run the numbers.

下一页，我们来计算一下数据。

Let’s imagine that every time my cousin participates in a skiing race, he has a two-in-ten chance of winning it, and a two-in-ten chance of breaking his knee. 2 How many races will he have won, on average, at the end of a championship consisting of ten races?

假设我的表弟每次参加滑雪比赛，都有十分之二的概率赢得比赛，也有十分之二的概率摔断膝盖。 2 在一个由十场比赛组成的锦标赛结束时，他平均会赢得多少场比赛？

The naïve answer is two races. That is the product of the number of races, ten, times the probability of winning each, two-in-ten. This would be correct if the race outcomes were independent of each other. However , if he breaks his knee during a race, he misses the following ones.

最简单的答案是两场比赛。也就是比赛场次（十场）乘以每场比赛的获胜概率（十分之二）。如果每场比赛的结果彼此独立，这个答案是正确的。然而，如果他在比赛中膝盖骨折，他就会错过接下来的比赛。

So , he can participate in the second race only if he didn’t injure his legs during the first one. He can participate in the third race only if he didn’t injure his legs in the previous two ones, and so on. His chances of completing all ten races are pretty slim – only 11%. 3 If we take the time to compute his chances to participate in each race, we discover that his expected number of wins is less than one. 4 This is fewer than the two wins we would expect if injuries didn’t prevent him from participating in subsequent races.

所以，他只有在第一场比赛中没有腿部受伤的情况下才能参加第二场比赛。他只有在前两场比赛中都没有腿部受伤的情况下才能参加第三场比赛，以此类推。他完成全部十场比赛的概率非常渺茫——只有11%。 3 如果我们计算他参加每场比赛的概率，我们会发现他预期获胜的次数不到一次。 4 这比我们预期他能赢得两次比赛的次数要少，因为伤病应该阻止他参加后续的比赛。

The point is, in a single instant of time, pure performance is all that matters. Instead , over a prolonged period of time, survival dwarfs performance.

关键在于，在某一瞬间，纯粹的表现至关重要。然而，从长远来看，生存远比表现重要。

# ↩

We can only observe the long-term outside of the short-term

我们只能在短期之外观察长期。

There is a difference between what matters when we consider narrow intervals and what does when we consider broader ones. Over the short term, consequences that apply beyond the short term do not matter. Over the long term, they do.

当我们考虑较短的时间跨度和较长的时间跨度时，需要考虑的因素有所不同。短期内，那些会影响到短期之后的后果并不重要；但从长远来看，它们至关重要。

In my cousin’s case, the broken leg preventing him from competing in future races is a “phantom consequence” that is not observable in the short term but affects the long term. If we make decisions based on what happens over narrow intervals and forget about these “phantom consequences,” we will make bad decisions. 5 Ergodicity is the study of these phantom consequences. 6

就我表弟而言，腿骨折使他无法参加未来的比赛，这是一种“隐性后果”，短期内无法观察到，但会影响长期。如果我们仅根据短期内发生的事情来做决定，而忽略这些“隐性后果”，我们就会做出错误的决定。遍历性正是研究这些隐性后果的学科。

# ↩

Irreversibility absorbs future gains

不可逆性会吸收未来的收益。

The explanation for the skier paradox is that, whereas my cousin had a chance to win each race, he is not guaranteed to race all of them. Any major injury prevents him from participating, causing him to forego expected future gains. 7

滑雪悖论的解释是，虽然我的表弟有机会赢得每一场比赛，但他并不能保证参加所有比赛。任何重大伤病都会使他无法参赛，导致他错失预期的未来收益。

In general, we can say that in any repeated activity, irreversibility absorbs future gains. This means that you cannot extrapolate future outcomes from solely the expected outcomes of the activity performed once. You also need to consider the impact of irreversible consequences.

一般来说，我们可以说，在任何重复性活动中，不可逆性都会抵消未来的收益。这意味着你不能仅仅根据一次活动的预期结果来推断未来的结果。你还需要考虑不可逆后果的影响。

For children, falls, fights, and mistakes in general tend to have more reversible consequences than for adults. Sometimes I wonder if part of the nostalgy for childhood is nostalgy for reversibility.

对孩子来说，摔倒、打架和各种错误造成的后果往往比成年人更容易逆转。有时我会想，人们对童年的怀念，是不是也包括对可逆性的怀念。

# ↩

Sustained performance

持续表现

Of course, what I mentioned so far is about long-term performance, not short-term performance. However , in many venues of life, the two are more similar than apparent.

当然，我前面提到的都是长期表现，而不是短期表现。然而，在生活的许多方面，这两者之间的相似之处远比表面看起来要多。

For example, winning a single race is an instance of short-term performance. However , to become a good enough racer to get admitted to the race and have a chance at winning it, long-term performance is necessary, too.

例如，赢得一场比赛属于短期表现。然而，要想成为一名足够优秀的赛车手，获得参赛资格并有机会赢得比赛，长期表现也必不可少。

Too often, we observe a snapshot of someone’s life and believe that we witnessed a piece of short-term performance. But if practice is required to get to a place where one can attempt that, then what we are really observing is long-term performance. A professional skier successfully managed risk in the previous decades – no matter what he seems to be doing in this one race we’re observing.

我们常常只看到某人人生中的某个瞬间，就以为自己目睹了某种短期表现。但如果达到那种水平需要练习，那么我们真正看到的其实是长期表现。一位职业滑雪运动员在过去几十年里成功地管理了风险——无论他在我们眼前这场比赛中的表现如何。

# ↩

Practical applications

实际应用

If you practice yoga, do not attempt to reach the maximum amount of stretch per session. 8 Instead , maximize the amount you can achieve without risking any major injury. 9 A single trauma is enough to prevent you from practicing effectively for months or even years.

如果你练习瑜伽，不要试图在每次练习中达到最大拉伸幅度。相反，应该在不造成严重损伤的前提下，尽可能地达到你能达到的最大拉伸幅度。一次小小的创伤就足以让你在数月甚至数年内无法有效地练习。

If you are a salesperson, do not attempt to make the most sales this quarter. Instead , aim to sell as much as possible without risking your reputation and your brand’s.

如果你是一名销售人员，不要试图在本季度完成最多的销售额。相反，你应该在不损害自身声誉和品牌形象的前提下，尽可能多地销售产品。

If you have a job, do not attempt to work as hard as possible. Instead , work as hard as you can without risking your health, marriage, or mental sanity. These three are damn hard to recover once lost. 10

如果你有工作，不要试图拼命工作。相反，要在不损害健康、婚姻或精神状态的前提下尽力工作。这三样东西一旦失去就很难挽回。

More in general, in any endeavor in which success depends on you accumulating some kind of resource (money, skill, connections, trust 11 , etc.), do not maximize growth regardless of survival. Instead , maximize growth that conserves survival.

更普遍地说，在任何成功取决于你积累某种资源（金钱、技能、人脉、信任等等）的事业中，不要不顾生存而追求最大化增长。相反，要追求在确保生存的前提下实现最大化增长。

# ↩

The sweet spot

最佳位置

The above is not an invitation to excessive prudence. Yes , until you experience pain, you do not know where the boundary is. And yes, going too slowly comes with problems, too.

以上并非提倡过度谨慎。的确，在经历痛苦之前，你无法真正了解界限在哪里。而且，行动过于缓慢也会带来问题。

Rather , the above is an invitation to distinguish between calculated risks whose consequences you can recover from and recklessness whose consequences might permanently debilitate you.

相反，以上内容旨在引导人们区分经过深思熟虑的风险（其后果可以恢复）和鲁莽行为（其后果可能会使你永久丧失行动能力）。

There is a sweet spot where you expose yourself to the former but not the latter 12 , and that’s a good place to aim.

存在一个最佳平衡点，既能让你接触到前者，又能避免后者，而这正是我们应该努力的方向。

Of course, easier said than done. Moreover , some people feel such a strong desire to achieve a risky goal that they might feel that not doing it would permanently debilitate them. That’s fine. This book wants to be informative, not prescriptive. It aims to give you the tools to make informed decisions, not to make decisions for you.

当然，说起来容易做起来难。此外，有些人渴望实现某个高风险目标，以至于他们觉得如果不去尝试就会终身受困。这也没关系。本书旨在提供信息，而非指导。它的目标是帮助你做出明智的决定，而不是替你做决定。

# ↩

The path forward

前进的道路

So far, I’ve talked about irreversibility in a rather abstract way. The next chapter presents a quantifiable example: Russian Roulette .

到目前为止，我对不可逆性的讨论都比较抽象。下一章将提供一个可量化的例子：俄罗斯轮盘赌。

1 I’m not saying that speed or performance doesn’t matter. It does. It just matters less than survival, given a long enough time frame.

我并不是说速度或表现不重要。它们当然重要。只是在足够长的时间尺度下，生存比速度或表现更重要。

2 Of course, these odds are greatly exaggerated, to show the point more clearly.

2 当然，这些概率被大大夸大了，目的是为了更清楚地说明这一点。

3 That would be 80% (the chances of safely completing a race) to the power of 10 (the number of races).

3 那将是 80%（安全完成比赛的概率）的 10 次方（比赛次数）。

4 The expected number of wins is ∑(0.8 i · 0.2), with i ranging from 1 to 10, where 0.8 is the chance of ending the race without an injury, and 0.2 is the chance of winning it. The result is 0.71 expected wins.

4. 预期获胜次数为∑(0.8 i · 0.2)，其中i的取值范围为1到10，0.8表示无伤完成比赛的概率，0.2表示赢得比赛的概率。结果为预期获胜次数0.71。

5 Good ideas make for some of the worst mistakes.

5. 好点子往往会导致最严重的错误。

6 Between others.

6. 其他人之间。

7 You can only expect average returns if you can play the game a large number of times – that’s what the law of large numbers is about. Therefore, if you want to get average returns, you should use a strategy that enables you to play the game a large number of times. This point will be further explored later.

7. 只有当你能够进行大量游戏时，才能期望获得平均收益——这就是大数定律的含义。因此，如果你想获得平均收益，就应该采用能够让你进行大量游戏的策略。这一点将在后面进一步探讨。

8 Yes, I know, yoga is much more than stretching. Still, the example holds for the stretching part.

8 是的，我知道，瑜伽远不止拉伸。不过，这个例子仍然适用于拉伸部分。

9 Or, better and wiser, focus on getting the input right rather than on maximizing the output. Practitioners will know what I mean.

9 或者，更明智、更恰当的做法是，专注于确保投入正确，而不是追求产出最大化。实践者会明白我的意思。

10 This doesn’t mean that hard work is bad. It’s not. Small stretches of extremely hard work are good and, in some professions, necessary. The problem is when there is no time for recovery, and damage accumulates until the inevitable breakdown.

10 这并不意味着努力工作不好。恰恰相反。短时间内极其辛苦的工作是有益的，在某些行业甚至是必要的。问题在于，当没有时间恢复时，损害就会不断累积，最终导致不可避免的崩溃。

11 Trust takes years to create and seconds to destroy, they say. True. And on top of that, trust takes personal closeness to create – if you break the trust someone put in you, you might be denied that closeness and thus the chances to rebuild trust .

人们常说，信任需要数年才能建立，却只需几秒钟就能摧毁。的确如此。而且，信任的建立需要亲密的个人关系——如果你辜负了别人对你的信任，你可能会失去这种亲密关系，也就失去了重建信任的机会。

12 Depending on the domain, in absolute terms, or relatively to the minimum reasonably possible to conduct the activity.

12 根据领域不同，可以绝对地，也可以相对地，以开展该活动所能合理达到的最低限度为限。

RUSSIAN ROULETTE

俄罗斯轮盘赌

I f you are reading this book, you probably never played Russian Roulette . It is a gambler’s game of the riskiest kind. The player takes a gun, empties the cylinder, and puts back a single bullet. Then , he spins the cylinder to randomize the position of the bullet. Finally , he takes the gun to his head. After staring at death for a few seconds, he pulls the trigger. If he survives, he collects a prize, usually in the tens of thousands of dollars. ( Obviously , do not try this at home, or anywhere else.)

如果你正在读这本书，你可能从未玩过俄罗斯轮盘赌。这是一种风险极高的赌博游戏。玩家拿起一把枪，清空弹仓，再装上一颗子弹。然后，他旋转弹仓，随机选择子弹的位置。最后，他把枪口对准自己的头部。在凝视死亡几秒钟后，他扣动扳机。如果他能活下来，就能赢得奖金，通常是数万美元。（显然，千万不要在家或其他任何地方尝试这种游戏。）

I’m telling you about Russian Roulette because some people are terrible at judging its odds. They then apply the same mistake to other areas of their lives, such as their relationships or careers, with disastrous consequences. Let’s see if you can guess better than them.

我之所以跟你讲俄罗斯轮盘赌，是因为有些人对它的赔率判断非常糟糕。然后，他们又把同样的错误运用到生活的其他方面，比如人际关系或事业上，结果往往是灾难性的。看看你能不能比他们猜得更准。

Usually , the game is played with a six-hole cylinder. This means that when the player pulls the trigger, he has a one-in-six chance of dying and a five-in-six chance of winning. Let’s imagine that the prize for a win is $6,000. How much money are you expected to win if you play Russian Roulette once?

通常，俄罗斯轮盘赌使用一个六孔轮盘。这意味着玩家扣动扳机后，有六分之一的概率死亡，五分之六的概率获胜。假设获胜奖金为 6000 美元。如果你玩一次俄罗斯轮盘赌，预计能赢多少钱？

The right answer is $5,000. That is the prize, $6,000, multiplied by the chances of winning, five-in-six. Now , a harder question. How much are you expected to win if you play Russian Roulette a hundred times?

正确答案是 5000 美元。这是奖金 6000 美元乘以中奖概率 5/6 的结果。现在，一个更难的问题：如果你玩 100 次俄罗斯轮盘赌，你预计能赢多少钱？

A back-of-the-napkin calculation would yield $500,000. That would be $5,000 (the expected winnings for a single play) multiplied by 100 (the number of plays). However , this answer is wrong.

粗略估算一下会得出50万美元的结论。这相当于5000美元（单次投注的预期奖金）乘以100（投注次数）。然而，这个答案是错误的。

The correct answer is about $0. After 100 rounds of Russian Roulette , you’re almost certainly dead and unable to collect any winning. 1

正确答案大约是 0 美元。玩了 100 轮俄罗斯轮盘赌后，你几乎肯定已经死了，也拿不到任何奖金了。

The chart below shows you the expected returns after playing Russian Roulette multiple times. As you can see, returns quickly plummet. 2

下图显示了多次玩俄罗斯轮盘赌后的预期收益。正如您所见，收益迅速下降。 2

This is because, in the beginning, winning a round increases your small winnings by a lot, but towards the end, you are already rich, and further wins add a small percentage to your wealth. Conversely , the chances of losing it all are constant at one-in-six and get harder and harder to avoid.

这是因为，一开始，赢一局能让你的小额奖金大幅增加；但到了后期，你已经相当富有，之后的胜利只会让你的财富增长一小部分。相反，输光所有钱的概率始终保持在六分之一，而且越往后越难避免。

The previous thought experiment comes from Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s “ Skin In The Game ” and clearly shows the link between ergodicity and irreversibility.

前一个思想实验来自纳西姆·尼古拉斯·塔勒布的《风险自负》，清楚地表明了遍历性和不可逆性之间的联系。

People who replied “$500,000” to the previous question assumed that death in one round just means that no winnings are collected during that round, but future rounds are still winnable. In Russian Roulette , however, one loss means that you also forego all future gains. Losses are irreversible and extend into the future.

对上一个问题回答“50万美元”的人认为，一轮死亡仅仅意味着该轮无法获得任何奖金，但之后的轮次仍然有机会获胜。然而，在俄罗斯轮盘赌中，一次失败意味着你将失去所有未来的收益。损失是不可逆转的，并且会影响到未来。

Sadly , relationships, careers, investments, and sports often share this undesirable property. For example, relationships are like Russian Roulette – in the sense that they grow stronger over time, but only if you get to spend time with your partner. If , one day, you break their trust, they might decide not to see you again. You will lose all chances to rebuild the relationship.

遗憾的是，人际关系、事业、投资和体育运动往往都具有这种令人担忧的特质。例如，人际关系就像俄罗斯轮盘赌——随着时间的推移，它会变得更加牢固，但这只有在你花时间陪伴伴侣的情况下才会发生。如果有一天你辜负了他们的信任，他们可能会决定不再见你。你将失去重建关系的所有机会。

Similarly , in investing, losing your capital means that you lost both your capital and all future returns that it could have generated.

同样，在投资中，损失本金意味着你不仅损失了本金，还损失了它本可以产生的所有未来收益。

# ↩

The path forward

前进的道路

If you feel slightly confused, don’t worry. It’s normal. Irreversibility is counterintuitive and goes against what we usually learn in school, that averages matter equally in the short- and in the long-term. This is seldom true. The next chapter explains why.

如果你感到有些困惑，别担心，这很正常。不可逆性与直觉相悖，也与我们通常在学校学到的“平均值在短期和长期都同样重要”的观念相悖。事实上，这种情况很少发生。下一章将解释其中的原因。

1 You only have a 12-in-a-billion chance of surviving 100 rounds of Russian Roulette.

1. 你在俄罗斯轮盘赌中活过 100 轮的概率只有十二亿分之一。

For comparison, you have a 16% chance of surviving 10 rounds and a 1% chance of surviving 25 rounds.

作为对比，你存活 10 轮的概率为 16%，存活 25 轮的概率为 1%。

In general, your chances of survival are (5/6) ^ n , where 5/6 are your chances of surviving one round, and n is the number of rounds played. Death over time is certain, that is, (5/6) n tends to zero for n → ∞.

一般来说，你的生存几率为 (5/6) ^ n，其中 5/6 是你存活一轮的几率，n 是游戏轮数。随着时间的推移，死亡是必然的，也就是说，当 n → ∞ 时，(5/6) n 趋于零。

2 In the first part of the curve, returns increase. This is because by playing an extra round, your total winnings increase by more than your probabilities of survival decrease. For example, by playing a second round, you can double your win but only decrease your chances of survival by one-in-six compared to playing once.

2. 在曲线的第一部分，收益会增加。这是因为多玩一轮，你的总奖金增加的幅度会超过生存概率的下降幅度。例如，玩第二轮，你的奖金可以翻倍，但与只玩一轮相比，你的生存概率只会下降六分之一。

However, after a bit, the returns stall, as in each round, you get to add a smaller and smaller percentage of your wealth, while your probabilities of losing it all are still 1/6. For example, by playing a sixth time, you only increase your winnings by 6/5, but your chances of survival decrease by one-in-six, a 5/6 multiplier. The two multipliers are reciprocal, so they cancel each other. Your rate of growth plateaus at 1.

然而，一段时间后，收益会停滞不前，因为每一轮你增加的财富比例都会越来越小，而输光所有财富的概率仍然是1/6。例如，玩第六轮，你的收益只会增加6/5，但你的生存概率却会降低1/6，也就是5/6的倍数。这两个倍数互为倒数，所以它们会相互抵消。你的增长率最终会稳定在1。

After that, the returns decrease. For example, by playing a seventh time, your winnings in case of survival become 7x instead of 6x, a 7/6 multiplier, but your chances of survival still decrease by one-in-six, a 5/6 multiplier. 7/6 multiplied by 5/6 makes 35/36, which is lower than one, so returns decrease. Afterward, it’s all downhill. Your rate of growth keeps decreasing: 40/42, 45/48, 50/54, …

之后，收益会递减。例如，玩第七次时，如果成功存活，你的奖金会从6倍变成7倍，也就是7/6倍，但你的存活几率仍然会降低六分之一，也就是5/6倍。7/6乘以5/6等于35/36，小于1，所以收益会递减。之后，情况就一路下滑。你的增长率会持续下降：40/42，45/48，50/54……

THE LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS

大数定律

I f you flip a coin, it will come out half of the time as heads and half of the time as tails. This is true if you flip it infinite times. However , if you only flip it ten times, it may come up six times as heads and four times as tails – a different result than the five and five expected. The fewer the flips, the higher the chances that the tally differs from the expected 50%. And the more coin flips are tallied, the more the average of observed results converges to the expected value. This is called the law of large numbers .

如果你抛一枚硬币，正面朝上的概率是50%，反面朝上的概率是50%。即使你抛无限次，这个规律依然成立。然而，如果你只抛十次，结果可能是正面朝上6次，反面朝上4次——这与预期的50%正面朝上50%的结果并不相同。抛掷次数越少，结果与预期的50%相差越大。而抛掷次数越多，观察到的结果的平均值就越接近预期值。这就是所谓的大数定律。

We generally assume the law of large numbers to be always relevant. In reality, it seldom is for individuals. It requires, well, a large number of trials. And in most real-life situations, we only have a limited number of them. For example, I cannot keep picking risky stocks until I get rich – a few bad results in a row, and I am broke.

我们通常认为大数定律总是适用的。但实际上，对于个人而言，它很少适用。它需要大量的试验。而在大多数现实生活中，我们只有有限的试验次数。例如，我不可能一直挑选高风险股票直到发财——连续几次失败，我就会破产。

Whenever an activity cannot be assumed to be repeatable at infinity, we should be wary of expecting to achieve its average outcome. 1

如果一项活动不能假定其无限重复，我们就应该谨慎对待期望达到其平均结果的预期。

# ↩

Game-over

游戏结束

In Russian Roulette , your expected earnings per trigger pulled are $5,000. However , if you are unable to pull it because you’re dead, your future earnings are effectively $0. You can only keep playing to win more money if you’re alive. Any form of “game-over” nullifies future gains, bringing the average down. 2

在俄罗斯轮盘赌中，每次触发按钮的预期收益为 5,000 美元。但是，如果您因为死亡而无法触发按钮，那么您未来的收益实际上为 0 美元。只有在您活着的时候，才能继续游戏并赢得更多奖金。任何形式的“游戏结束”都会使未来的收益归零，从而降低平均收益。

Similarly , in my cousin’s example, breaking his leg is a form of game-over (the damage is irreversible, at least during the championship). It implies losing the race in which the injury took place and all the following ones. This causes his average number of wins during a championship to be lower than expected (his chances of winning a race multiplied by the number of races).

同样，以我表弟为例，腿骨折就意味着比赛结束（至少在锦标赛期间，伤势是不可逆的）。这意味着他不仅输掉了受伤的那场比赛，还输掉了之后的所有比赛。这导致他在整个锦标赛期间的平均胜场数低于预期（他赢得比赛的概率乘以比赛场次）。

When “permanent game-overs are possible,” do not rely on averages. 3

当“游戏可能永久结束”时，不要依赖平均值。

# ↩

Many kinds of game-over

多种游戏结束方式

Game -overs are common. They include bankruptcies, injuries, severe depression, burnouts, and break-ups of all kinds (between romantic partners, business partners, or friends). The next chapter analyzes some of them.

人生终结很常见，包括破产、受伤、重度抑郁、职业倦怠以及各种形式的分手（情侣、商业伙伴或朋友之间的分手）。下一章将分析其中的一些终结。

1 This includes both intrinsic limits to how many times we can repeat the activity (e.g., after my cousin broke his legs a few times, he couldn’t ski anymore) and extrinsic ones (e.g., a professional skiing career only lasts a couple of decades, after which one is too old).

1 这包括我们重复某项活动次数的内在限制（例如，我的表弟几次摔断腿后就不能再滑雪了）和外在限制（例如，职业滑雪生涯只有几十年，之后就太老了）。

2 Hence, we can say that possible game-overs are a cause of non-ergodicity.

2 因此，我们可以说，可能的游戏结束是非遍历性的原因。

3 It doesn’t mean averages don’t matter, but that one must ask how likely the average is to apply to himself.

3 这并不意味着平均值不重要，而是说人们必须问自己，平均值有多大可能适用于自己。

# ↩
5
# ↩

MUCH OF LIFE IS A RUSSIAN ROULETTE

人生很多时候就像一场俄罗斯轮盘赌。

T he last two chapters put a lot of emphasis on the mechanics of Russian Roulette . You might have wondered, “ Great , but I’m not a gambler. Why should I care about Russian Roulette ?”

最后两章重点讲解了俄罗斯轮盘赌的机制。你可能会想：“很好，但我又不是赌徒，我为什么要关心俄罗斯轮盘赌呢？”

The thing is, much of life follows similar mechanics, in which losses absorb future gains. I already mentioned how, in relationships, breaking trust might prevent any future attempt to rebuild the connection. Here are a couple more examples.

事实上，生活中很多事情都遵循类似的机制，损失会抵消未来的收益。我之前已经提到过，在人际关系中，信任的破裂可能会阻碍未来重建关系的任何尝试。这里还有几个例子。

– Sports . The harder you practice, the faster you progress. However , if you try too hard, you might injure yourself. Irrecoverable damage to your joints might end your ability to perform the sport well, or at all.

——体育运动。练习越刻苦，进步越快。然而，过度训练可能会导致受伤。关节的不可逆损伤可能会彻底断送你从事这项运动的能力，甚至让你无法继续从事这项运动。

– Career . The harder you work, the more chances you have for professional success. However , if you work too many hours for too long, you might endanger your health, marriage, or mental sanity. Once lost, these are hard, if not impossible, to recover from.

事业方面，你越努力，获得职业成功的机会就越大。然而，如果工作时间过长，可能会危及你的健康、婚姻或精神状态。一旦失去这些，即使不是完全无法挽回，也很难恢复。

A single negative event can render short-term maximization irrelevant.

一次负面事件就可能使短期利益最大化变得无关紧要。

# ↩

Prudence, not cowardice

谨慎，而非怯懦

The presence of irreversibility doesn’t imply that you should not take any risk (after all, it’s risky not to take any risk). Instead , it means that you should acknowledge the non-ergodicity of the context at hand and take risks in a way that does not seriously impair your future if things go wrong.

不可逆性的存在并不意味着你不应该承担任何风险（毕竟，不承担任何风险本身就是一种风险）。相反，它意味着你应该认识到当前情境的非遍历性，并以一种即使结果不尽如人意也不会对你的未来造成严重损害的方式来承担风险。

Prudence , not cowardice.

谨慎，而非怯懦。

# ↩

The costs of short-term performance

短期绩效的成本

We saw how a single negative event can render short-term maximization irrelevant.

我们看到，一次负面事件就能使短期利益最大化变得无关紧要。

Hence , when measuring short-term performance, we should always account for the costs of the risks eventual optimization carried, regardless of whether they have manifested yet.

因此，在衡量短期绩效时，我们应该始终考虑最终优化所带来的风险成本，无论这些风险是否已经显现。

* * *

The second part of this book contains three strategies to use. It will also show you that prudence, when done right, is not just a way to minimize downsides but to enable upsides, too.

本书第二部分介绍了三种策略。它还将向您展示，谨慎行事如果运用得当，不仅可以最大限度地减少不利影响，还能带来有利结果。

Before that, let’s work towards the definition of ergodicity. The next chapter will introduce two key terms: lifetime outcome and population outcome. Their difference is of paramount importance.

在此之前，我们先来探讨遍历性的定义。下一章将介绍两个关键术语：终生结果和群体结果。它们之间的区别至关重要。

# ↩
6
# ↩

POPULATION AND LIFETIME OUTCOMES

人口与终生结果

E arlier on, I introduced the gambler’s game of Russian Roulette . As a reminder, a player has a one-in-six chance of dying and a five-in-six chance of winning a prize, let’s say, $6,000.

前面我介绍了赌徒们玩的俄罗斯轮盘赌游戏。简单来说，玩家有六分之一的概率死亡，也有六分之五的概率赢得奖金，比如说6000美元。

In Russian Roulette , the outcome of a person playing it a few times is different from the average outcome of a few people playing it once. Let’s compute each.

在俄罗斯轮盘赌中，一个人玩几次的结果与几个人玩一次的平均结果不同。让我们分别计算一下。

Let’s say that six people play Russian Roulette once each. The prize is $6,000. On average, one person will die, and five will win $6,000. The group as a whole obtained one death and $30,000. Divided by the number of participants, 6, it makes 1/6 of a death and $5,000. That is the expected outcome.

假设六个人每人玩一次俄罗斯轮盘赌。奖金是 6000 美元。平均而言，一人会死，五人会赢得 6000 美元。整个群体共计一人死亡，五人赢得 6000 美元。除以参与人数 6，得出 1/6 的死亡人数和 5000 美元。这就是预期结果。

This expectation remains correct if we increase the number of gamblers. With 600 gamblers, you will have an average of 100 deaths and $3M. Divided by 600 people, it still makes 1/6 of a death and $5,000. Therefore , the expected outcome is also called the population outcome. 1

如果增加赌徒人数，这个预期仍然成立。600 名赌徒平均会有 100 人死亡，损失 300 万美元。除以 600 人，仍然是 1/6 人死亡，损失 5000 美元。因此，预期结果也称为总体结果。

Your individual expected outcome if you play Russian Roulette once is also 1/6 of a death and $5,000. However , if you play it more than once, it begins to decrease. If you play it an infinite number of times, you will be dead for sure. Your final outcome, what you can walk away with, is $0 and a hole in your head.

如果你玩一次俄罗斯轮盘赌，你的预期结果是六分之一的概率会死，外加5000美元。但是，如果你玩不止一次，这个概率就会开始下降。如果你无限次地玩，你肯定会死。你最终能带走的，也就是0美元和一颗子弹。

The chart shows how your expected financial gains from playing Russian Roulette many times are roughly zero. I call this expectation, measured across one person and many repetitions, the lifetime outcome. Its technical name is time average or time probability. 2

图表显示，多次玩俄罗斯轮盘赌的预期收益几乎为零。我将这种基于个人多次重复游戏的预期收益称为“终身收益”。它的专业术语是时间平均值或时间概率。

I spent a few pages describing the difference between population and lifetime outcomes because they are the key to defining ergodicity. In particular,

我花了些篇幅来描述人口结果和终生结果之间的区别，因为它们是定义遍历性的关键。特别是，

A system is ergodic 3 if its population outcome coincides with the lifetime outcome of each of its components. Otherwise , it is non-ergodic.

如果一个系统的总体结果与其每个组成部分的生命周期结果一致，则称该系统是遍历的 3 。否则，该系统是非遍历的。

# ↩

The practical implication

实际意义

The practical implication is that in ergodic systems, you can use the population outcome to make optimal decisions. In non-ergodic systems, you cannot. ( On an only partially related note, I often joke that 5 in 6 economists think that Russian Roulette is safe.)

实际意义在于，在遍历系统中，你可以利用总体结果做出最优决策。在非遍历系统中，则不能。（顺便提一句，我经常开玩笑说，六分之五的经济学家认为俄罗斯轮盘赌是安全的。）

For example, Russian Roulette is non-ergodic because the lifetime outcome differs from the population outcome. If you keep playing it because you fail to grasp its non-ergodicity and mistakenly believe that your lifetime outcome equals your population one, you will end up dead instead of rich.

例如，俄罗斯轮盘赌是非遍历的，因为个人的最终结果与总体结果不同。如果你因为未能理解其非遍历性而继续玩下去，错误地认为你的个人结果等于总体结果，那么你最终会丧命而不是致富。

Hence the purpose of this book. By teaching you the implications of non-ergodic contexts and how to recognize them, I seek to help you avoid irreversible mistakes whose importance is clear only after the fact – a bit like my cousin learned with his injury.

因此，本书的目的就在于此。通过讲解非遍历性语境的含义以及如何识别它们，我希望帮助你避免那些事后才意识到其重要性的不可挽回的错误——就像我表弟受伤后所学到的那样。

1 Sometimes also called the ensemble average .

1 有时也称为集合平均值。

2 I use the term “lifetime outcome,” even though not canonical, as I have experienced it leads to faster understanding.

2 我使用“终身结果”这个术语，尽管它并非规范术语，但根据我的经验，它有助于更快地理解。

3 Across this book, I use the expression “a system is ergodic” as a shorthand for “a model describing a system is ergodic.” The later chapter on the definition of ergodicity explains this choice.

3 在本书中，我使用“系统是遍历的”这一表达作为“描述系统的模型是遍历的”的简写。后面关于遍历性定义的章节将解释这种选择。

7
# ↩

RISK AVERSION

风险规避

T here is a common belief that people are irrationally risk averse. It the result of experiments such as the following.

人们普遍认为，人们天生具有非理性的风险规避倾向。以下实验结果证实了这一点。

“ Here is a game. You flip a coin. If it’s heads, I give you $1000. If it’s tails, you give me $950. Do you want to participate?”

“我们来玩个游戏。你抛硬币。正面朝上，我给你1000美元；反面朝上，你给我950美元。你想参加吗？”

From a logical-naïve point of view, the expected return of playing the bet is $1000 times 50% (the chances of winning) minus $950 times 50% (the chances of losing). That would be $500 - $475 = $25. On average, every time you play the game, you’re expected to win $25. This makes the gamble apparently desirable. And yet, if researchers go around asking the question to real people, most decline. This led behavioral economists to conclude that people are irrationally risk-averse. Are they, though? 1

从逻辑上简单的角度来看，参与赌博的预期收益是 1000 美元乘以 50%（获胜概率）减去 950 美元乘以 50%（失败概率）。也就是 500 美元 - 475 美元 = 25 美元。平均而言，每次参与赌博，预期收益都是 25 美元。这使得赌博看起来颇具吸引力。然而，如果研究人员向普通民众询问这个问题，大多数人都会拒绝参与。这使得行为经济学家得出结论：人们天生具有非理性的风险规避倾向。但事实真是如此吗？

If people had infinite cash, they could play the game as long as they wanted. The law of large numbers would kick in, their lifetime outcome would converge to their expected outcome, and they would realize the expected win of $25 per coin flipped.

如果人们拥有无限的资金，他们就可以随心所欲地玩这个游戏。大数定律会发挥作用，他们最终的收益会趋近于预期收益，他们最终会实现每次抛硬币25美元的预期收益。

However , real people do not have infinite cash. They can only play this game a few times before emptying their bank accounts or having to quit the game. Some cannot even afford to lose once.

然而，现实生活中人们的钱是有限的。他们玩这款游戏几次之后，要么会输光所有积蓄，要么就只能退出游戏。有些人甚至一次都输不起。

For real people, the limitation on the number of times they can play can transform their lifetime outcome of a gamble into negative.

对于普通人来说，赌博次数的限制可能会使他们一生的赌博结果变成负面的。

The next page shows an example.

下一页展示了一个例子。

Imagine that you have a prosperous sum of $1000 in your pocket. After one iteration of the game,

想象一下，你口袋里有1000美元。游戏进行一轮后，

– you might have won the toss and won $1000.

——你可能赢得了掷硬币，并赢得了 1000 美元。

– you might have lost the toss and lost $950.

——你可能输了掷硬币，损失了950美元。

The average is a win of $25, as expected. However , if you are offered to play a second time, you can only afford to play if you win the first toss. Therefore , you can expect to win $25 from the second toss only if you won the first one. This means that in four parallel universes,

平均每次掷硬币可赢25美元，正如预期。然而，如果让你玩第二次，你只有在第一次掷硬币获胜的情况下才能负担得起第二次掷硬币。因此，只有当你赢得第一次掷硬币时，你才能期望从第二次掷硬币中赢得25美元。这意味着在四个平行宇宙中，

– In the first, you won both tosses, and you’re up by $2000.

– 第一局，你两次掷硬币都赢了，赢了 2000 美元。

– In the second, you won the first toss and lost the second one. You’re up $50.

– 第二局，你第一次掷硬币赢了，第二次输了。你赢了50美元。

– In the third, you lost the first toss and cannot play again. You’re down $950.

第三局，你第一轮掷硬币就输了，不能再玩了。你输了950美元。

– In the fourth, you also lost the first toss and cannot play again. You’re down $950.

– 第四局，你第一次掷硬币也输了，不能再玩了。你输了950美元。

After two iterations of the game, you have won an average of just ($2000 + $50 - $950 -$950) / 4 = $37.5

经过两轮游戏，你平均只赢了（2000美元 + 50美元 - 950美元 - 950美元）/ 4 = 37.5美元。

This is surprising! If you had infinite wealth, you would have won an average of $25 per bet times two equals $50. But because your wealth is finite, your average win is lower: only $37.5

这真是令人惊讶！如果你拥有无限的财富，你平均每次下注能赢25美元，乘以2就是50美元。但由于你的财富是有限的，你的平均赢利会更低：只有37.5美元。

More importantly, you have a one-in-four chance of winning a lot of money, one-in-four chances of winning a modest amount, and one-in-two chances of losing a significant amount. This means that you have a one-in-two chance of being yelled at by your spouse and/or hurt in your self-esteem in exchange for a mere $37.5 expected winnings 2 . Not a choice that any rational person would take.

更重要的是，你有四分之一的概率赢得一大笔钱，四分之一的概率赢得一笔数额不大的钱，还有二分之一的概率输掉一大笔钱。这意味着，你只有二分之一的概率会因为区区37.5美元的预期收益而被配偶责骂，或者自尊心受到打击。任何理性的人都不会做出这样的选择。

Actually , it would be idiotic to volunteer to play a game with these odds. The behavioral economists who called for “irrational risk-aversion” are the irrational ones.

事实上，在这种赔率下自愿参加游戏简直是愚蠢至极。那些鼓吹“非理性风险规避”的行为经济学家才是真正不理性的人。

Further readings: Ole Peters ’ papers 3 discuss this problem and contain additional examples of how (non-)ergodicity explains the hidden rationality of some risk aversion and of other behaviors that would be irrational in an ideal ergodic world. As far as I know, he was the first to propose ergodicity as the solution to many otherwise puzzling behaviors.

延伸阅读：Ole Peters 的论文 3 讨论了这个问题，并提供了更多例子，说明（非）遍历性如何解释某些风险规避行为以及其他在理想遍历世界中会被视为非理性的行为的内在理性。据我所知，他是第一个提出遍历性可以解释许多其他令人费解的行为的人。

1 Cunning readers might have thought that such a bet is suspicious. Whoever proposes it must be a swindler; hence, it is wise to decline playing. This is sound reasoning and, by itself, a good enough reason to explain the hesitancy of participants. However, as the next page will show, even assuming full good faith in the person proposing the bet, it is still advised to refuse to play it.

1. 精明的读者或许会觉得这样的赌局很可疑。提议者一定是骗子；因此，拒绝参与是明智之举。这种想法合情合理，也足以解释参与者的犹豫不决。然而，正如下一页将要阐述的，即便假设提议者完全出于善意，仍然建议拒绝参与。

2 Assuming a limit of two plays and $1000 cash in the wallet before beginning the game.

2 假设最多只能玩两次，并且在游戏开始前钱包里有 1000 美元现金。

The more the plays, the lower the average winnings.

游戏次数越多，平均盈利越低。

3 I recommend https://ergodicityeconomics.files.wordpress.com/2018/06/ergodicity_economics.pdf

3 我推荐 https://ergodicityeconomics.files.wordpress.com/2018/06/ergodicity_economics.pdf

8
# ↩

WHAT YOU SEE IS NOT ALL THERE IS

你所看到的并非全部。

D eep down, we already know that survival matters. Our instincts scream not to go down the hill that fast, not to work overtime every day risking burnout, and not to risk betraying the trust of our friends and neighbors.

内心深处，我们都知道生存至关重要。我们的本能会警告我们不要走得太快，不要每天加班冒着精疲力竭的风险，也不要辜负朋友和邻居的信任。

Sadly , when we observe someone’s success, our automatic reaction is often to desire it for ourselves, without asking ourselves if we would actually like it – both its pros and its cons , without cherry-picking.

可悲的是，当我们看到别人成功时，我们的第一反应往往是渴望自己也能成功，却不去问问自己是否真的喜欢它——它的优点和缺点，而不是只挑着看。

Entrepreneur and philosopher Naval Ravikant wisely noted that envy is most often an illusion. “ The part of the person that we envy doesn’t exist without the rest of that person,” he writes. “ If we aren’t willing to trade places with them completely – their life, their body, their thoughts – then there is nothing to be envious of.”

企业家兼哲学家纳瓦尔·拉维坎特睿智地指出，嫉妒往往是一种错觉。他写道：“我们嫉妒的那部分人，离不开这个人本身。如果我们不愿意与他们完全交换——他们的生活、他们的身体、他们的思想——那么就没有什么值得嫉妒的。”

I would add that it is also pointless to envy someone with whom you wouldn’t trade places in all parallel universes – including those in which his gambles didn’t pay off. For example, an entrepreneur whose venture had slim chances to succeed. 1 Do you desire to take his gambles, or do you only desire the winning outcome?

我还要补充一点，嫉妒一个你无论身处哪个平行宇宙都不愿意和他交换位置的人毫无意义——即使是在他冒险失败的那些宇宙里。例如，一个创业成功几率渺茫的企业家。你是渴望承担他那样的冒险，还是只想要最终的胜利？

Do not envy the survivors of ventures in which you don’t wish to participate, and do not envy successes that don’t reproduce well. 2

不要羡慕那些在你不愿参与的事业中幸存下来的人，也不要羡慕那些无法复制的成功案例。

It’s easy to envy the lottery winner and harder to envy the whole population of lottery players.

人们很容易羡慕彩票中奖者，但很难羡慕所有彩民。

# ↩

Survivorship bias

幸存者偏差

Michigan truck driver Mark Clark won four million dollars at the lottery. Twice , in 2017 and 2020.

密歇根州卡车司机马克·克拉克两次赢得彩票大奖，分别在2017年和2020年，奖金高达四百万美元。

Does it make him the greatest investor ever?

这是否意味着他是史上最伟大的投资者？

It is hard to make higher returns than the man who won the lottery twice. Yet , that doesn’t mean that his strategy is worth imitating.

想要获得比两次中彩票的人更高的回报很难，但这并不意味着他的策略值得效仿。

Too often, when we look at the winner, we fail to see all his clones in the parallel universes in which he lost his bets. Any serious decision-making process cannot neglect them.

我们常常只关注赢家，却忽略了在平行宇宙中那些输掉赌注的“克隆人”。任何严肃的决策过程都不能忽视他们。

Whenever we desire an outcome because we see those who benefited from it, it is good practice to ask yourself, do you want the outcome, or do you want the opportunity to take the gamble that produced the outcome? If you only want the former but not the latter, you might be unprepared for what’s to come.

当我们因为看到某些人从中受益而渴望某种结果时，最好问问自己：你是想要这个结果，还是想要承担产生这个结果的风险的机会？如果你只想要前者而不要后者，那么你可能对即将发生的事情毫无准备。

* * *

“ Fortune favors the living brave.”

JED TROTT

“机遇总是眷顾勇敢的活着的人。”——杰德·特罗特

Most of the braves who are still around for us to observe did benefit from their acts of courage. But rigor demands that we extend our study to all braves – both those who survived and those who perished.

我们现在还能见到的大多数勇士都因他们的英勇行为而受益。但严谨的研究要求我们将研究范围扩大到所有勇士——无论他们是幸存者还是牺牲者。

1 In this case, it is useful to distinguish between the case of an entrepreneur who succeeds against all odds because others were wrong in guessing the odds, and the case of one who took a bet that heavily relied on luck.

1 在这种情况下，区分以下两种情况很有必要：一种是企业家克服重重困难取得成功，因为其他人对成功的概率估计错误；另一种是企业家下注，而这种赌注很大程度上依赖于运气。

In the second case, I do not want to take away any merit – society benefits from entrepreneurs taking gambles with individual downside and societal upside, so I’m grateful for his actions. That said, I am also wary of envying him. I can envy his decision if and only if I would desire to take the gamble he took, not just his win.

在第二种情况下，我并不想否定他的做法——社会受益于企业家承担个人风险和社会收益的冒险精神，所以我很感激他的行为。话虽如此，我也不敢对他产生嫉妒之情。只有当我渴望承担他所承担的风险，而不仅仅是他所取得的成功时，我才能真正羡慕他的决定。

2 This doesn’t mean not to take them – pursuing them might be a good strategy, if you can take enough of them to ~guarantee that at least one will succeed. This strategy is explored later in the book.

2 这并不意味着不要尝试——如果你能尝试足够多的尝试，确保至少有一个成功，那么尝试这些尝试或许是个不错的策略。本书后面会详细探讨这个策略。

PAYOFFS CHANGE AS TIME HORIZONS CHANGE

随着时间跨度的变化，收益也会发生变化。

T ake two skiers. The first one has a 20% chance of winning each race and a 10% chance of breaking his leg during that race. The second one takes fewer risks; as a result, he has a 15% chance of winning each race but only a 1% chance of breaking his leg.

假设有两个滑雪运动员。第一个运动员每场比赛有20%的概率获胜，同时也有10%的概率在比赛中摔断腿。第二个运动员风险较小，因此他每场比赛有15%的概率获胜，但摔断腿的概率只有1%。

Which skier will win more races during a championship?

在锦标赛中，哪位滑雪运动员会赢得更多比赛？

Take a couple of seconds to answer, then move to the next page.

请花几秒钟时间回答，然后继续下一页。

The right answer is that it depends on how long the championship is.

正确答案是，这取决于锦标赛的赛程有多长。

If it comprises a single race, the first skier – the risk-taking one – has a higher number of expected wins: 0.18 vs. 0.15 (each is the product of the chances of finishing a race times the chances of winning it; for example, 90% times 20% makes 0.18). However , the more races in the championship, the higher the chances that the first skier will break his leg and has to forfeit the remaining races. In fact, if we run the numbers (see the table below) , we can see that the risk-taking skier wins more races than the conservative one in championships up to five races long. Any longer than that, and the conservative approach pays more.

如果比赛只有一轮，那么第一个滑行的滑雪者——也就是冒险型滑雪者——预期获胜次数更高：0.18 对 0.15（这两个数值都是完成比赛的概率乘以获胜概率的乘积；例如，90% 乘以 20% 等于 0.18）。然而，锦标赛的比赛轮数越多，第一个滑行的滑雪者腿部骨折而不得不放弃剩余比赛的概率就越高。事实上，如果我们计算一下（见下表），我们可以看到，在比赛轮数不超过五轮的锦标赛中，冒险型滑雪者比保守型滑雪者赢得的比赛更多。但如果比赛轮数超过五轮，保守型滑雪者的优势就更大了。

What’s the takeaway? That payoffs depend on time horizons .

结论是什么？收益取决于时间跨度。

And what’s the practical implication? That you cannot base your decisions on a payoff computed on a time horizon that isn’t yours.

那实际意义是什么呢？这意味着你不能根据一个与你自身时间范围不同的时间范围计算出的收益来做决定。

Never assume that a strategy that’s optimal for a time horizon is also optimal for all time horizons.

永远不要想当然地认为在某个时间范围内最优的策略也是所有时间范围内最优的。

THE POINT SO FAR

目前为止的重点

H ere are a few key points covered so far:

以下是目前为止讨论的一些要点：

  • Irreversibility absorbs future gains.
    不可逆性会吞噬未来的收益。
  • We call “population outcome” the outcome of many people performing an action once, and “lifetime outcome” the outcome of one person performing an action many times. If they differ, the system that produces them is non-ergodic.
    我们称“群体结果”为许多人执行一次操作的结果，称“终身结果”为一个人多次执行同一操作的结果。如果二者不同，则产生这些结果的系统是非遍历的。
  • You can only rely on expected outcomes if you are guaranteed a large number of repetitions. Otherwise , they are misleading. ( The law of large numbers requires a large number of repetitions).
    只有在保证大量重复实验的情况下，预期结果才能被信任。否则，它们会产生误导。（大数定律要求进行大量重复实验。）
  • Risk aversion is rational in the presence of non-ergodicity.
    在非遍历性的情况下，规避风险是理性的。

WHAT WORKS ON AVERAGE CAN STILL FAIL LOCALLY

平均而言行之有效的方法，在局部范围内仍可能失效。

In the first part of this book, we learned that what happens in the short term does not necessarily describe what happens in the long term, even if the conditions do not change over time .

本书第一部分中我们了解到，即使条件没有随时间改变，短期内发生的事情也不一定能描述长期内发生的事情。

In the second part of this book, we will extend the concept of irreversibility through space. We will see how, for example, a public service might work well on average and yet fail locally.

本书第二部分将不可逆性的概念扩展到空间层面。我们将探讨例如公共服务如何在平均层面运行良好，但在局部层面却可能出现故障。

Then , we will extend irreversibility through the layers of society, and talk about incentives at the group level. We will see how caring for someone doesn’t necessarily translate into doing what’s best for them.

接下来，我们将把不可逆性扩展到社会各个层面，并探讨群体层面的激励机制。我们将看到，关心他人并不一定意味着会去做对他们最有利的事情。

Finally , we will move to the third part of this book, where you will receive a definition of ergodicity.

最后，我们将进入本书的第三部分，您将在这里看到遍历性的定义。

ONE VS. MANY

一对多

I live in Turin , Italy . It’s a quiet metropolis at the foot of the mountains. From there, it’s a short ride to Bergamo province, the hardest-hit by the 2020 coronavirus pandemic. So many people died there because the hospitals got overwhelmed. Many perished in their houses because they couldn’t access medical attention.

我住在意大利都灵。这是一座坐落在山脚下的宁静大都市。从那里出发，驱车不远即可到达贝加莫省，那里是2020年新冠疫情的重灾区。由于医院不堪重负，许多人因此丧生。还有许多人因为无法获得医疗救助而死在家中。

And yet, on average, the healthcare system worked great. On average, hospitals didn’t see many coronavirus hospitalizations. On the worst day of the pandemic, only about 10% of Italian public hospital beds were occupied by coronavirus patients. 1

然而，总体而言，医疗系统运转良好。平均而言，医院收治的新冠肺炎患者并不多。在疫情最严重的一天，意大利公立医院的床位占用率也只有约10%，且均收治了新冠肺炎患者。

Of course, average data does not tell us the full story. If every hospital in Italy had 10% of their beds occupied by patients, everyone would have gotten proper medical attention. The problem was that patients predominantly lived in the same region. A few hospitals got completely overwhelmed, while those in other regions didn’t.

当然，平均数据并不能反映全貌。如果意大利每家医院的床位占用率都达到10%，那么所有患者都能得到妥善的医疗救治。问题在于，患者大多居住在同一地区。少数几家医院不堪重负，而其他地区的医院则没有出现这种情况。

A system can work well on average and still fail locally.

一个系统平均而言可能运行良好，但局部仍可能出现故障。

# ↩

The assumption of independence

独立性假设

We saw that, in non-ergodic contexts, irreversibility limits the number of trials over time, preventing the law of large numbers from applying.

我们看到，在非遍历环境中，不可逆性限制了试验次数，从而阻止了大数定律的应用。

Similarly , we can extend the law of large numbers and its limitations not just through time but also through space and populations. 2 The law of large numbers expects that the larger a population of people performing an action, the closer the average outcome is to the expected average. For example, 75% heads is not a surprising outcome if four people flip a coin (three people flipped heads and one flipped tails). However , if four hundred people flip a coin, the average outcome is much more likely to be 50%, or 51%, or some percentage around that.

同样，我们可以将大数定律及其局限性扩展到时间、空间和人口等多个维度。大数定律指出，参与某项行动的人数越多，平均结果就越接近预期平均值。例如，如果四个人抛硬币（其中三人抛出正面，一人抛出反面），75% 的正面朝上并不令人惊讶。然而，如果四百人抛硬币，平均结果更有可能是 50%、51% 或接近这个百分比。

This happens because the coin results are independent. Your neighbor’s result does not influence yours. However , in most of real life, what occurs to your neighbors does influence what happens to you.

这是因为每次抛硬币的结果都是独立的。你邻居的抛硬币结果不会影响你的结果。然而，在现实生活中，邻居的遭遇确实会影响你的遭遇。

For example, we can expect the victims of pandemics and natural disasters to be located near each other. Therefore , we cannot rely on national averages to assess whether the emergency systems are ready. Instead , we must consider local workload spikes.

例如，我们可以预见，疫情和自然灾害的受害者往往分布在彼此附近。因此，我们不能依赖全国平均水平来评估应急系统是否准备就绪。相反，我们必须考虑局部地区的工作量高峰。

* * *

# ↩

On the news, we saw the pain of the families in the hardest-hit areas. People died because the overcrowded local hospitals couldn’t admit them.

新闻报道中，我们看到了受灾最严重地区家庭的痛苦。许多人因为当地医院人满为患而无法收治病人，最终不幸离世。

As an individual, you do not care whether the system works on average. You care if it works for you.

作为个人，你并不关心系统平均而言是否有效，你只关心它是否对你有效。

A test on the average time it takes for an ambulance to reach a patient gives little information on how long it takes for two ambulances to reach the same point.

对救护车到达病人平均所需时间的测试，对于两辆救护车到达同一地点所需时间的比较，提供的信息并不多。

The lesson: averages might hide local spikes in irreversibility. This is problematic when survival is based on the local. In such cases, aggregate evaluations cannot substitute local ones.

教训是：平均值可能会掩盖不可逆性中的局部峰值。当生存取决于局部因素时，这会造成问题。在这种情况下，总体评估不能替代局部评估。

1 29,010 COVID hospitalizations on the 4th of April in Italy, and 284,713 public hospital beds in Italy according to an untitled report on the Italian Health Ministry website ( link ). I’m writing these lines in September 2020.

根据意大利卫生部网站上一份未命名的报告（链接），截至4月4日，意大利共有129,010例新冠肺炎住院病例，以及284,713张公立医院床位。我写下这些文字时是2020年9月。

2 Informally.

2 非正式地。

CENTRALIZATION

集权

T his tension between what happens on average and what happens locally is a core problem of centralization. Centralized organizations such as the WHO or the EU are not omniscient nor have unlimited bandwidth. Their executives cannot read tons of data that describe every corner of the world. They must rely on averages. They cannot make thousands of micro-decisions, each appropriate for a given corner of the world. They must take a single, one-fits-all decision. 1

平均情况与局部情况之间的这种矛盾是集中化的核心问题。像世界卫生组织或欧盟这样的集中式组织并非全知全能，也没有无限的资源。它们的管理者无法阅读描述世界每个角落的大量数据。他们必须依赖平均值。他们无法做出成千上万个针对世界特定角落的微观决策。他们必须做出一个适用于所有情况的单一决策。

Even if these decisions work on average, they might have a terrible impact on some local populations. 2 As we saw previously, something working on average doesn’t imply it works.

即使这些决策平均而言是有效的，它们也可能对某些地方居民造成可怕的影响。正如我们之前看到的，平均而言有效的方法并不意味着它一定有效。

Let me repeat: something working on average doesn’t imply it works. Hospitals don’t work when they work on average; they work when they work for everyone, all the time. The same is true for schools, institutions, social services, public transportation, production lines, and much more.

我再说一遍：平均而言有效的事物并不意味着它就有效。医院并非平均而言有效，而是当它对所有人、在任何时候都有效时才有效。学校、机构、社会服务、公共交通、生产线等等，都是如此。

Averages are useful metrics, but they cannot be the only ones. Centralized institutions must be particularly careful not to over-rely on them.

平均值是有用的指标，但不能作为唯一的指标。集中式机构尤其需要注意，不要过度依赖平均值。

# ↩

Centralization and efficiency

集中化和效率

Central organizations tend to receive more input and feedback from people geographically, socially, or culturally close to them. Those living at the geographic, social, or cultural peripheries are often ignored by central organizations. Just think about how company vice presidents tend to discuss other vice presidents’ problems more frequently than those of line workers, how governments tend to spend more time discussing urban problems than rural ones, and how school systems tend to discuss intellectual matters more often than practical ones.

中心化组织往往更容易收到来自地理位置、社会或文化背景与自身接近的人们的意见和反馈。而那些生活在地理、社会或文化边缘地带的人们则常常被中心化组织忽视。想想看，公司副总裁们往往更频繁地讨论其他副总裁的问题，而不是一线员工的问题；政府往往花更多时间讨论城市问题，而不是农村问题；学校系统往往更频繁地讨论理论问题，而不是实践问题。

The closer geographically, socially, and culturally your governors are to you, the more likely they are to work on what you care. 3

你的执政者在地理、社会和文化上与你越接近，他们就越有可能致力于你所关心的事情。

Hence , centralization is only efficient for the central observer.

因此，集中化仅对中心观察者有效。

The closer someone lives to the capital, and the more their culture and social status match those of the governors, the more they care about what the central organization is good at and the less they care about what it’s bad at.

一个人居住的地方离首都越近，其文化和社会地位与统治者越相符，就越关心中央机构擅长什么，而越不关心中央机构不擅长什么。

When evaluating centralization, make sure you ask everyone, not just those close to you.

在评估集中化程度时，一定要询问所有人，而不仅仅是与你关系密切的人。

# ↩

Practical applications

实际应用

Be wary of centralization, especially when there is no skin in the game ensuring that the incentives of the center coincide with those of the peripheries. 4

要警惕中心化，尤其是在缺乏利益攸关方来确保中心与边缘的利益一致的情况下。

Good intentions and being part of the same country or organization are not enough. Even assuming good faith and competence, the center cannot possibly fathom all consequences of its actions on the periphery, nor has any good way to measure that in a non-superficial way.

良好的意愿以及同属一个国家或组织是不够的。即使假设中心拥有善意和能力，它也无法完全预见其行为在周边地区的所有后果，也没有任何有效的方法可以客观地衡量这些后果。

The Hungarian Parliament , beautiful. One challenge of centralized decision making is ensuring that the center is well in touch with the periphery. This is hard, as in many countries, a representative from the periphery has more in common with other representatives from other regions than with his constituents.

匈牙利议会大厦真漂亮。集中决策的一大挑战在于如何确保中央与地方保持密切联系。这并非易事，因为在许多国家，来自地方的代表往往与其他地区的代表的共同点远多于与选民的共同点。

# ↩

Capillarity

毛细作用

Consider our circulatory system, or a plant’s, both of which have a capillary structure.

想想我们的循环系统，或者植物的循环系统，它们都具有毛细血管结构。

The capillary structure of a leaf.

叶片的毛细结构。

Our heart pumps blood into arteries, which then divide into vessels and then capillaries. This is because blood cells can only exchange oxygen with those tissue cells that are nearby.

我们的心脏将血液泵入动脉，动脉再分支成血管，最后形成毛细血管。这是因为血细胞只能与附近的组织细胞进行氧气交换。

The same happens in all large systems: change can only be driven by people who are close to those they want to change, and some information about problems and needs can only be collected by those who personally know those having them. Hence , large countries and organizations should have a capillary structure where information isn’t collected nor pushed at scale, directly linking the center to the peripheries, but rather step-by-step, layer-by-layer, between people who know each other’s context well.

所有大型系统都遵循同样的规律：变革只能由与目标群体关系密切的人推动，而关于问题和需求的信息也只能由那些与问题和需求相关的人亲自收集。因此，大型国家和组织应该采用毛细管式结构，信息并非大规模收集或推送，直接连接中心和边缘，而是通过彼此了解情况的人，一步一步、层层传递。

# ↩

Granularity

粒度

A major problem of centralization is the lack of granularity. A central government cannot possibly review granular data and cannot enact policies that are granular enough to be effective everywhere. Instead , we get one-fits-all.

集中化的一个主要问题是缺乏精细化。中央政府不可能审查精细的数据，也无法制定足够精细以在所有地方都有效的政策。因此，我们只能得到一刀切的政策。

Hence , it is important to bring decision-making closer to the people involved – e.g., if a decision can be made at the provincial or state level, it should be made at the provincial level.

因此，让决策更贴近相关人员非常重要——例如，如果可以在省或州一级做出决定，就应该在省一级做出决定。

A common critique is that “decisions taken at lower levels are inefficient for they lack economies of scale.” However , they more than make up for it with the benefits of tailoring. They provide more of what would be good for the province and less of what would be bad. Isn’t this efficiency?

一种常见的批评是，“基层决策效率低下，因为缺乏规模经济。”然而，它们通过量身定制的优势弥补了这一不足。它们提供了更多对省份有利的因素，减少了不利因素。这难道不是效率吗？

1 In early 2020, the WHO and other centralized health institutions condemned effective measures such as face masks on the grounds that not everyone has them – a position I call “minimum common denominator healthcare.”

2020 年初，世界卫生组织和其他中央卫生机构谴责了口罩等有效措施，理由是并非每个人都有口罩——我称之为“最低公分母医疗保健”。

2 Institutions such as the EU make much more sense in an ergodic world than in a non-ergodic one.

2. 像欧盟这样的机构在遍历世界中比在非遍历世界中更有意义。

3 Many disagreements between people in good faith come from one of the following two causes: they’re optimizing different metrics, or they’re considering the marginal utility of a resource whose utility is nonlinear and of which they possess different quantities (e.g., $100 is less important to a millionaire than to a single parent working a part-time job – of course, they will have different perceptions of the value of $100, even if none is virtue signaling).

3 许多出于善意的人们之间的分歧源于以下两个原因之一：他们优化的是不同的指标，或者他们考虑的是某种资源的边际效用，而这种资源的效用是非线性的，并且他们拥有的数量也不同（例如，100 美元对百万富翁来说不如对做兼职的单亲父母重要——当然，他们对 100 美元的价值的看法会不同，即使没有人是在炫耀美德）。

4 The idea of electing representatives of the periphery to become part of the center was supposed to solve the problem. It would, in theory, but only if the representatives were true members of the periphery and, after a short mandate, had to come back and be members of the periphery again. Sadly, I am witnessing more and more that the representatives elected in the peripheries are members of the center – not geographically but socially and culturally.

4. 选举边缘地区的代表成为中心的一部分，这一想法原本旨在解决问题。理论上确实如此，但前提是这些代表必须是真正的边缘地区成员，并且在任期结束后必须回到边缘地区。令人遗憾的是，我越来越发现，在边缘地区选出的代表实际上是中心地区的成员——并非地理意义上的中心，而是社会和文化意义上的中心。

THE AVERAGE RETURNS AREN’T YOUR RETURNS

平均收益并不等同于您的收益

D id you ever miss a plane because the train to the airport was late?

你有没有因为去机场的火车晚点而错过飞机的经历？

It happened to me. I didn’t get any relief from the train company’s apology, noting that the average delay for their trains was only one minute. I did not care about the average. I only cared about my train having been 30 minutes late, making me miss my plane.

这事儿也发生在我身上了。铁路公司道歉说他们列车的平均延误时间只有一分钟，但这并没有让我释怀。我根本不在乎平均延误时间，我只在乎我的火车晚点了30分钟，害我错过了飞机。

Averages are misleading. As we already saw, systems might work on average and still fail locally.

平均值具有误导性。正如我们已经看到的，系统平均而言可能运行良好，但在局部范围内仍可能出现故障。

# ↩

# ↩

IRREVERSIBILITY

不可逆性

A verages are a meaningful metric only when future gains offset past losses. It is often not the case. Continuing the previous example, I do not care if, next time, the train arrives 30 minutes in advance. I do not get a free flight when the train arrives in advance. Arriving in advance doesn’t offset a delay if it doesn’t offset its consequences.

只有当未来的收益能够弥补过去的损失时，平均值才是一个有意义的指标。但这种情况往往并非如此。继续之前的例子，我并不在意下次火车是否提前30分钟到达。火车提前到达并不会让我免费乘飞机。如果提前到达不能弥补延误造成的后果，那么它就无法弥补延误。

As a rule of thumb, we cannot rely on averages whenever there is a possibility for irreversible damage. 1 This is because the possibility of irreversible damage makes a context non-ergodic.

一般来说，当存在不可逆损害的可能性时，我们不能依赖平均值。这是因为不可逆损害的可能性使得上下文成为非遍历的。

When we consider averages, the good offsets the bad. However , for individuals, something good happening to someone else doesn’t offset the bad that happened to them, nor does something good happening to them offset something bad having happened to them in the past, not always. 2

当我们考虑平均值时，好事可以抵消坏事。然而，对于个人而言，发生在别人身上的好事并不能抵消自己曾经遭遇的坏事，同样，发生在自己身上的好事也不能抵消自己过去曾经遭遇的坏事，并非总是如此。

# ↩

Practical applications

实际应用

If you find yourself in a non-ergodic context, do not care about the average outcome but about your own. Do not rely on averages but on probabilities of irreversible individual outcomes.

如果你身处非遍历性情境，不要关心平均结果，而要关心你自己的结果。不要依赖平均值，而要依赖不可逆个体结果的概率。

Use more granular data. Ask yourself what might happen to you. Ask yourself if and how unexpected losses can negate your future plans.

使用更细致的数据。问问自己可能会发生什么。问问自己意外损失是否以及如何会破坏你的未来计划。

For example, do not invest all your money in the one investment with the highest average return. Instead , consider what would happen in case of a downturn. Do not care about average returns – only about those with which you could end up.

例如，不要把所有钱都投入到平均收益率最高的单一投资项目上。相反，要考虑市场低迷时会发生什么。不要只关注平均收益率，而要关注最终的收益。

1 Readers versed in ergodicity will know that it’s not just about irreversible damage, but any forms of irreversibility.

熟悉遍历性的读者会知道，这不仅仅是关于不可逆转的损害，而是任何形式的不可逆转性。

2 This point is in addition to the previous one that irreversibility absorbs future gains. A bankrupt investor loses the possibility of benefiting from the following market growth. And a divorced husband loses the possibility of restoring the relationship.

2 这一点与前一点相辅相成，即不可逆性会吞噬未来的收益。破产的投资者失去了从后续市场增长中获利的机会。离婚的丈夫也失去了修复婚姻关系的机会。

THE GAMBLER AND THE GAMBLE

赌徒与赌博

H ow do you make money in the start-up business?

在创业过程中如何赚钱？

If you are an investor, the go-to strategy is the following. Place many bets by investing in a lot of promising companies. Push them to grow as fast as possible. Many will fail. One or two will become wildly successful, making hundreds of times your money back. These will recoup the losses on all the other companies, leaving you with enough profits to drink Mai Tais on a beach for the rest of your life.

如果你是一名投资者，最常用的策略是这样的：投资大量有潜力的公司，尽可能地分散投资。推动它们快速发展。很多公司会失败，但其中一两家会取得巨大成功，让你获得数百倍的回报。这些成功将弥补你在其他公司上的损失，让你余生都能在海滩上悠闲地喝着迈泰鸡尾酒。

That’s a great strategy to make money in the start-up business, for wealthy investors. Not so much for founders. Many would prefer a strategy where they are likely to end up with a moderately successful company rather than a lottery ticket to be the next Zuckerberg .

对于富有的投资者来说，这的确是创业领域赚钱的好策略。但对于创始人而言，却未必如此。许多人更倾向于选择一种更有可能最终拥有一家小有成就的公司，而不是寄希望于成为下一个扎克伯格的碰运气策略。

Of course, it’s not so black and white. Many founders do make good money, live exciting years, and gain experience and connections. The point is, the best strategy depends on whether you are the gambler or the gamble. If you are the gambler, you do not care about each gamble making money. You care about the aggregate of all gambles making money. Conversely , if you are the gamble (in this example, the founder), you do not care about the overall outcome of all gambles but only yours.

当然，事情并非如此非黑即白。许多创始人确实赚到了丰厚的财富，度过了精彩的岁月，并积累了经验和人脉。关键在于，最佳策略取决于你是赌徒还是赌徒本身。如果你是赌徒，你并不关心每次赌博是否盈利，你关心的是所有赌博的总盈利情况。相反，如果你是赌徒本身（在本例中，指创始人），你并不关心所有赌博的最终结果，而只关心你自己的赌博是否盈利。

# ↩

You: a gambler

你：一个赌徒

Even if you do not play gambling games, it might be useful to see yourself as a gambler. After all, each of your habits is a gamble in which you bet time and energy for a possible return. Similarly , any belief of yours is a gamble. Any job of yours, any relationship of yours, any idea, any decision – they are all investments of time and money in exchange for a future return. 1

即使你不玩赌博游戏，把自己看作一个赌徒或许也很有帮助。毕竟，你的每一个习惯都是一种赌博，你投入时间和精力去换取可能的回报。同样，你的任何信念也是一种赌博。你的任何工作、任何关系、任何想法、任何决定——它们都是对时间和金钱的投资，以换取未来的回报。

You might be tempted to strive to win any single gamble of yours. Don’t . As long as your strategy involves investing in a portfolio of gambles, you can afford to let go of a few losing ones. Their survival is not necessary for yours. 2 In fact, letting natural selection act upon your gambles is how you adapt, thus reducing the chances you’ll be a victim of natural selection yourself.

你或许会想方设法赢得每一场赌博。千万别这么做。只要你的策略是投资于一系列赌博项目，你就可以承受放弃一些亏损的项目。它们的存亡与你的存亡无关。事实上，让自然选择作用于你的赌博项目，才是你适应环境的方式，从而降低你自身成为自然选择牺牲品的概率。

Remember , the best strategy for the gamble isn’t necessarily the best strategy for the gambler. 3

记住，对赌局来说最好的策略，未必对赌徒来说也是最好的策略。

# ↩

Replaceable, for whom?

可以被取代吗？对谁来说？

This chapter made the point that sharing a stake in the same venture isn’t a guarantee of alignment. Parties might still have different incentives and different opinions on what is replaceable and what is not.

本章指出，共同投资同一企业并不能保证目标一致。各方仍可能存在不同的利益诉求，对哪些资产可以替代、哪些资产不可替代也持有不同的看法。

This pattern is everywhere in nature and society. For an employee, their own career and health are irreplaceable, but for the company, most employees are replaceable. Firings and employee burnout are part of doing business. 4 5

这种模式在自然界和社会中随处可见。对员工而言，自己的职业生涯和健康是不可替代的，但对公司而言，大多数员工都是可以替代的。解雇和员工倦怠是商业运作的一部分。

For a mother, her child is irreplaceable. Instead , for the species, natural selection means an improvement.

对母亲而言，孩子是无可替代的。而对物种而言，自然选择意味着进化。

For a soldier, his life and those of his squad brothers are irreplaceable. For a general, losing a few soldiers is a painful cost that might be worth paying to win the war.

对一名士兵来说，他和战友的生命是无可替代的。对一位将军来说，损失几名士兵是痛苦的代价，但为了赢得战争，这代价或许是值得的。

In general, the survival of a population does not coincide with the survival of its members, not all of them. 6 7

一般来说，一个种群的存续并不等同于其所有成员的存续，并非所有成员都能存续。

Of course, this applies only to some contexts. We can call them “non-ergodic.” This is not a complete nor precise definition of ergodicity. However , it is a valuable one, for it provides an important distinction. In non-ergodic contexts, you cannot be idealistic and believe that your survival coincides with that of your company or country. You must take additional steps to take care of yourself.

当然，这仅适用于某些情况。我们可以称之为“非遍历性”。这并非遍历性的完整或精确定义，但它很有价值，因为它提供了一个重要的区别。在非遍历性情境中，你不能理想化地认为你的生存与公司或国家的生存息息相关。你必须采取额外的措施来保护自己。

War memorials are often erected to reconcile

战争纪念碑的建立通常是为了和解。

As an example, I have many friends working in consulting. Their job is hard, and their employers squeeze every bit of productivity out of them. Most went through burnout. It is to be expected. Their company has little to lose from their burnout, or less than they do. Their incentives are not as aligned as it seems, even though the employees are part of the company, and both value survival.

举个例子，我有很多朋友在咨询公司工作。他们的工作很辛苦，雇主会榨干他们的每一分生产力。大多数人都经历过职业倦怠。这很正常。他们的公司从他们的倦怠中损失不大，或者说损失比他们自己还小。尽管员工是公司的一份子，双方都重视生存，但实际上他们的利益并不像表面看起来那么一致。

The question is, does non-ergodicity apply to the relationship between them and their company? Yes . Then , they must acknowledge that they and their company have different incentives. They have two alternatives. One , realign incentives – for example, by becoming irreplaceable. 8 Two , acknowledge that they need a plan B .

问题是，非遍历性是否适用于他们与公司之间的关系？答案是肯定的。那么，他们必须承认自己和公司的激励机制不同。他们有两种选择。第一，重新调整激励机制——例如，让自己变得不可替代。第二，承认他们需要一个备选方案。

This is not about ethics. The point is that a population doesn’t have, by default, an incentive for the survival of all its members. Even if the population means good for its members – especially so. A population must first and foremost ensure its survival to guarantee the survival of its members. And if the survival of the population doesn’t coincide with the survival of all its members – as is the case in non-ergodic conditions –, a well-meaning population won’t necessarily guarantee the survival of all its members, not when it comes at the cost of its own survival.

这并非关乎伦理道德。关键在于，一个群体并非天生就具有保障所有成员生存的动力。即便这个群体真心希望所有成员都能生存下去——尤其如此。一个群体必须首先确保自身的生存，才能保障其成员的生存。如果群体的生存与所有成员的生存并不一致——例如在非遍历条件下——那么，即使这个群体出于善意，也未必会保障所有成员的生存，尤其是在这会以牺牲自身生存为代价的情况下。

For example, when facing external threats that put at risk the survival of the whole population, some sacrifices might become necessary. Or , as another example, when the survival of the most decadent or freeloading members of the society might endanger its existence.

例如，当面临危及全体人口生存的外部威胁时，做出一些牺牲可能是必要的。又例如，当社会中最堕落或最不负责任的成员的生存可能危及整个社会的存亡时，也需要做出一些牺牲。

For a company or a population, the replaceability of its members means ergodicity. For the individual members, the opposite applies.

对于公司或群体而言，其成员的可替代性意味着遍历性。对于个体成员而言，情况则相反。

# ↩

The implication

这意味着

As an individual, you cannot blindly rely on membership in a group for your survival. Instead , become an irreplaceable part of it. This way, the group deems your loss irrecoverable and acts to prevent it at all costs . 9

作为个体，你不能盲目地依赖群体成员身份来求得生存。相反，你应该成为群体中不可或缺的一部分。这样，群体就会认为你的离开是无法挽回的，并会不惜一切代价阻止这种情况发生。

# ↩

Burn your habits before they burn you

在你被恶习灼伤之前，先烧掉你的恶习！

Natural selection benefits populations. This is good news if you are a population and bad news if you are one of its weak members.

自然选择有利于种群。如果你是种群中的一员，这是好消息；但如果你是种群中的弱势成员，这则消息就不妙了。

In the latter case, you can turn the tables by making natural selection work for you rather than against you. The trick is to become a population yourself. This is easier than it seems – after all, you already are a population: of habits and beliefs. If you let the feedback you receive from your environment hurt the habits and beliefs that are holding you back, you are effectively making natural selection act inside you rather than on you. 10 You become stronger rather than extinct.

在后一种情况下，你可以通过让自然选择为你所用而不是与你对抗来扭转局面。诀窍在于让自己成为一个群体。这比看起来要容易——毕竟，你本身就是一个群体：由习惯和信念构成。如果你让来自环境的反馈伤害那些阻碍你前进的习惯和信念，你实际上是在让自然选择作用于你的内部而不是外部。你会变得更强大，而不是被淘汰。

You are not your habits nor your beliefs. You are their container. Their survival is not yours. What’s best for them might or might not be what’s best for you.

你并非你的习惯或信仰，你只是它们的容器。它们的生存与你的生存无关。对他们而言最好的，未必对你而言是最好的。

10 In my “Antifragile Organizations” workshop, I teach managers and entrepreneurs that while change and natural selection are inevitable, they can influence the level at which it will happen: upon their company (bad) or within it (good), upon their employees (bad for the employees) or within them (good for them).

10 在我的“反脆弱组织”研讨会上，我教导管理者和企业家，虽然变革和自然选择是不可避免的，但他们可以影响变革发生的程度：发生在他们的公司（不好）或公司内部（好），发生在他们的员工身上（对员工不利）或发生在他们自身身上（对他们有利）。

Much of becoming more antifragile is about pulling adaptation forward in time (by adapting before it’s too late) and pushing it down across layers (so that we adapt within us before the system adapts by getting rid of us).

增强反脆弱性的关键在于提前适应（在为时已晚之前进行适应），并将其向下推行到各个层面（以便在系统通过消灭我们而进行适应之前，我们自身先进行适应）。

# ↩

THE POINT SO FAR

目前为止的重点

O ver the previous pages, we have seen three “paradoxes” of non-ergodicity.

在前几页中，我们已经看到了非遍历性的三个“悖论”。

  1. Survival matters more than performance for long-term performance.
    从长远来看，生存比业绩更重要。
  2. Something can work on average and still fail, carrying irreversible losses.
    某种东西平均而言可能有效，但仍然可能失败，造成不可挽回的损失。
  3. What’s best for the survival of the individual isn’t necessarily what’s best for the survival of the population, and the other way around.
    对个体生存最有利的，不一定对种群生存最有利，反之亦然。

All three assertions only apply to non-ergodic contexts. Hence , the importance of understanding ergodicity. Whether you are in an ergodic world or not determines what is rational and what isn’t.

这三个论断都仅适用于非遍历性情境。因此，理解遍历性至关重要。你是否身处遍历性世界，决定了什么是理性的，什么是不理性的。

Now , let’s define ergodicity.

现在，让我们来定义遍历性。

遍历性

The last three parts of this book detail practical strategies to guide your actions in non-ergodic contexts.

DEFINING ERGODICITY

遍历性的定义

# ↩

A simple definition of ergodicity

遍历性的简单定义

A system 1 is ergodic if, for all its components, the lifetime outcome corresponds to the population outcome.

如果对于系统 1 的所有组成部分，其生命周期结果与人口结果相对应，则称该系统是遍历的。

Otherwise , it is non-ergodic. 2

否则，它是非遍历的。

# ↩

Practical applications

实际应用

Do not trust advice about a non-ergodic context that assumes it is ergodic. While evaluating advice, always ask yourself if it assumes ergodicity. If so, how would things change, removing that assumption?

不要轻信那些假设非遍历环境是遍历环境的建议。在评估建议时，务必问问自己：它是否假设了遍历性？如果是，那么去掉这个假设，情况会如何变化？

Fully relying on averages and expected outcomes makes sense only in ergodic contexts. In non-ergodic ones, you want to ensure that you make decisions based on an estimate of your lifetime outcome. 3

完全依赖平均值和预期结果只有在遍历性情境下才有意义。在非遍历性情境下，你需要确保你的决策是基于对终生结果的估计。

Similarly , when we see a behavior that we deem illogical or irrational, it is often worth asking ourselves, “ Is it irrational for an ergodic world but rational for a non-ergodic one?”

同样地，当我们看到某种我们认为不合逻辑或不理性的行为时，我们常常值得问问自己：“对于遍历世界来说，它是不理性的，但对于非遍历世界来说，它是理性的吗？”

# ↩

A more technical definition of ergodicity

遍历性的更技术性定义

Here are a few, sometimes alternative, sometimes complementary, definitions of ergodicity.

以下是遍历性的几个定义，有时是替代性的，有时是补充性的。

Using the words of Ole Peters and Alexander Adamou , 4

借用奥勒·彼得斯和亚历山大·阿达穆的话， 4

An observable […] is called ergodic if its expectation value is constant in time and its time average converges to this value with probability one.

如果一个可观测量的期望值随时间保持不变，并且其时间平均值以概率 1 收敛到该值，则称该可观测量是遍历的。

( Author’s note: a reminder that expectation value and time average correspond to population and average outcome, respectively.)

（作者注：提醒一下，期望值和时间平均值分别对应于总体和平均结果。）

Using the words of an anonymous blogger by the name of Spear of Lugh , 5

借用一位名为斯皮尔·卢格的匿名博主的话， 5

Ergodicity is verified if, more or less, every time that you compute a statistical measurement (across space or time), you find the same result. It means that randomness is “well shared.” Another way to see it is that when you have ergodicity, doing N random experiments in parallel will give you the same result as doing N experiments one after the other.

如果每次计算统计测量值（跨越空间或时间）时，都能得到大致相同的结果，则可验证遍历性。这意味着随机性“共享良好”。换句话说，当系统具有遍历性时，并行进行 N 次随机实验与依次进行 N 次实验会得到相同的结果。

1 Or, more precisely, ergodicity is the property of a mathematical model describing a system. In particular, the adjective “ergodic” should refer to an observable in a mathematical model, as Ole Peters pointed out (https://twitter.com/ole_b_peters/status/1293499007663308800?s=20).

1 或者更准确地说，遍历性是描述系统的数学模型的性质。特别是，形容词“遍历的”应该指数学模型中的可观察对象，正如 Ole Peters 指出的那样（https://twitter.com/ole_b_peters/status/1293499007663308800?s=20）。

That said, for the sake of clarity, in this book, I will frequently use the adjective “non-ergodic” in relation to a system. This is because, in most practical examples relevant to the real world, it is plausibly impossible to come up with a model representative of real life in which the system described is ergodic, at least in the context at hand. Most fully-ergodic human activities belong to casinos or casino-like settings, and, no, I won’t consider a casino representative of real life.

尽管如此，为了表述清晰，本书中我将频繁使用“非遍历性”这个形容词来描述系统。这是因为，在大多数与现实世界相关的实际例子中，我们几乎不可能找到一个能够代表现实生活的模型，使得所描述的系统至少在当前语境下是遍历性的。大多数完全遍历性的人类活动都发生在赌场或类似赌场的环境中，而我当然不会将赌场视为现实生活的代表。

2 Here, I provided the simplest definition I could come with that applies to most practical cases, favoring clarity over precision. The next pages contain a more technical and precise definition.

2 在这里，我提供了一个尽可能简单易懂的定义，它适用于大多数实际情况，我更注重清晰性而非精确性。接下来的几页将提供一个更专业、更精确的定义。

3 Bearing in mind the considerations of the later chapter, “non-binary ergodicity,” – real life is made of shades, tradeoffs, and careful balances, not binary considerations.

3 考虑到后面章节“非二元遍历性”的考虑——现实生活是由细微差别、权衡取舍和谨慎的平衡构成的，而不是二元考虑。

4 https://ergodicityeconomics.files.wordpress.com/2018/06/ergodicity_economics.pdf

4 https://ergodicityeconomics.files.wordpress.com/2018/06/ergodicity_economics.pdf

5 https://spearoflugh.substack.com/p/ergodicity-and-digital-culture-13ba17989890

5 https://spearoflugh.substack.com/p/ergodicity-and-digital-culture-13ba17989890
